children: Airline major IndiGo is using a network of 28 bonded stations as well as major gateways such as Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru to connect domestic cargo with international markets.

Speaking to businessline, Mark Sutch, CCO–CarGo and Head of International Development, said the airline’s domestic reach provides an opportunity to connect Indian businesses with overseas markets and support international carriers seeking access beyond the country’s main gateways.

“Through major gateways such as Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru, supported by 28 bonded stations across the country, we are increasingly able to connect domestic cargo flows with international markets and vice versa,” Sutch said.
“Our extensive domestic footprint also positions us as a valuable partner for global airlines seeking access to markets beyond India’s primary gateways.”

The domestic cargo, Sutch said, remains the foundation of IndiGo’s cargo business, while international cargo is emerging as an important growth driver, supported by its expanding network and long-haul capabilities.

Besides its own operations, the airline is widening its reach through partnerships with Virgin Cargo and Air France KLM Martinair Cargo. These arrangements provide access to markets beyond IndiGo’s network.
The airline carried approximately 4.5 lakh tonnes of cargo in FY26, compared with 3.87 lakh tonnes in FY25.
IndiGo expects volumes to reach 1.5–2 times the FY26 level by FY30, supported by domestic and international network expansion.
Furthermore, Sutch said India’s location between major manufacturing hubs, consumption markets and trade corridors provides an opportunity to develop the country into a cargo transshipment hub.
However, he emphasised that geography alone would not be sufficient.
“Successful hub positioning requires efficient cargo processing, reliable cold-chain infrastructure, seamless transit procedures, and competitive pricing,” he said.
According to Sutch, diversifying supply chains and congestion at traditional cargo hubs create opportunities for India to capture a larger share of international cargo flows.
Meanwhile, continued infrastructure development and supportive policy measures would be important to this effort, he said.
At present, IndiGo operates three dedicated A321 freighters, which complement the belly-cargo capacity available across its passenger network.
The freighters primarily support international cargo flows and seasonal requirements where dedicated capacity adds value.
Accordingly, these deployments are guided by demand, trade patterns, shipment characteristics, network connectivity and aircraft availability.
The airline has recently commenced freighter services from Navi Mumbai and Kochi to Sharjah.
Additionally, the induction of Airbus A350 aircraft from 2028 is expected to significantly increase IndiGo’s cargo-carrying capacity on longer routes.

In addition, Sutch said widebody belly-hold capacity would support higher-value and time-sensitive shipments, including pharmaceuticals, automotive components, advanced manufacturing products and perishables.

As such the planned fleet of 60 A350 aircraft would also open access to new global trade flows, with cargo expected to play a larger role in supporting the economics of IndiGo’s expanding international network.

title: IndiGo taps 28 bonded stations to connect domestic cargo with global markets
